title: About
text:
What. MHDSR (Methods in Health Data Science with R) is a live, cohort-based training pathway in applied biostatistics and machine learning for health research, taught in R with reproducible Quarto workflows. It comprises three courses, a base course (BIOSTATR), an advanced course (ML4HOR), and a meta-analysis course (METAR), that can be taken independently or followed as a pathway.








Figure 1: The MHDSR pathway




Each course can be taken independently, but ML4HOR and METAR assume the level of R covered in BIOSTATR.


 Why
Health researchers are often taught statistics and R as separate subjects, disconnected from the reproducible workflows expected in publication and clinical practice. MHDSR closes that gap: every course pairs the underlying methodology with a hands-on R implementation and ends with a reproducible Quarto report.


 Who it’s for
Clinicians, researchers, PhD students, public health professionals, and analysts who want a rigorous, hands-on introduction to modern health data analysis in R. No advanced statistics background is required for BIOSTATR; ML4HOR and METAR build on it but can be taken independently.


 What you get
Live sessions, slides, notebooks, datasets, and exercises for every session, with direct feedback in a small cohort, ending in a short reproducible Quarto mini-project.

title: ML4HOR
text:
ML4HOR


Machine Learning for Health Outcomes with RPrediction



 18 hours · 9 sessions · 3 weeks  28/09 – 16/10/2026  200€ (2000 MAD)





Course description
ML4HOR is the advanced course of the MHDSR pathway: a practical introduction to machine learning for health outcomes research using R. It covers the full supervised workflow (from classic models to boosting and neural networks), unsupervised learning and clustering for patient phenotyping, honest tuning and model selection, evaluation and validation, and interpretability.
The final sessions move from analysis to a reproducible ML pipeline driven by a command-line agent, including LLM-assisted tasks such as structured extraction and text classification, with their limits and guardrails.
The course emphasizes validation, data-leakage prevention, appropriate performance metrics, calibration, interpretability, and clinical relevance.


Learning objectives
By the end of ML4HOR, participants will be able to:

frame supervised and unsupervised problems in health outcomes research;
prepare tabular health datasets and avoid data leakage;
apply clustering for patient phenotyping and subgroup discovery;
fit penalized regression, tree ensembles, boosting, and multilayer perceptrons;
tune and select models with nested cross-validation and fair comparison;
evaluate discrimination, calibration, and clinical usefulness, and choose thresholds;
validate models internally and externally;
interpret models with permutation importance, PDP/ICE, and SHAP;
drive a reproducible ML pipeline with a command-line agent under version control;
use LLMs for structured extraction and text classification, and assess their outputs.





Schedule



No.


Session




1


Machine learning fundamentals: supervised vs unsupervised, bias-variance, train/test, cross-validation, resampling




2


Data preparation: preprocessing, missing data, encoding, standardization, feature engineering, data leakage




3


Unsupervised learning and clustering: distances, k-means, hierarchical clustering, choosing K, silhouette, stability, PCA for exploration and visualization




4


Classic supervised models: penalized regression, decision trees, random forests




5


Boosting and neural networks: gradient boosting, multilayer perceptron, regularization, early stopping, model comparison




6


Model tuning and selection: hyperparameters, grid/random search, nested cross-validation, overfitting




7


Evaluation and validation: AUC, sensitivity/specificity, PPV/NPV, F1, calibration, Brier score, thresholds, internal/external validation




8


Interpretability: variable importance, permutation importance, PDP/ICE, SHAP, local vs global interpretation




9


Agents, LLMs and a reproducible ML pipeline: CLI agent, code generation/execution/review, versioning, structured extraction, LLM classification, limits and guardrails





Practical information



Audience


Researchers, PhD students, clinicians, public health professionals, data analysts


Prerequisites


Basic R and statistical literacy, as covered in BIOSTATR

title: MHDSR
text:
Programme design
The MHDSR pathway has three courses. BIOSTATR is the base course: R and data manipulation, descriptive statistics, inference, linear and logistic regression, survival analysis and flexible survival models, missing data and multiple imputation, and meta-analysis, all with reproducible R/Quarto workflows. ML4HOR is the advanced course: supervised learning from classic models to boosting and neural networks, unsupervised learning and clustering, tuning and validation, interpretability, and a reproducible ML pipeline driven by a command-line agent. METAR is a focused course in conducting meta-analysis: review protocol and search strategy, effect sizes, fixed- and random-effects models, heterogeneity, forest plots, meta-regression, publication bias, and certainty of evidence.
Each course can be taken independently, but ML4HOR and METAR assume the level of R covered in BIOSTATR.

title: BIOSTATR
text:
BIOSTATR


Applied Biostatistics with RFoundations



 18 hours · 9 sessions · 3 weeks  19/10 – 06/11/2026  200€ (2000 MAD)





Course description
BIOSTATR is the base course of the MHDSR pathway: a practical, rigorous introduction to applied biostatistics for health research using R. It takes participants from a clean R and data-manipulation workflow through inference, regression, survival analysis, missing-data handling, and meta-analysis, all with reproducible Quarto reporting.
No statistics or programming background is required. The course emphasizes estimation, interpretation, reproducibility, and the appropriate use of statistical methods in clinical research. Meta-analysis is taught here as a biostatistical method, not as a review-methodology course.


Learning objectives
By the end of BIOSTATR, participants will be able to:

organize a reproducible analysis with R, Quarto, and version control;
import, clean, reshape, and quality-check health datasets;
summarize and visualize health data appropriately, including stratified summaries;
interpret confidence intervals, p-values, effect sizes, power, and sample size;
compare groups with suitable tests for quantitative and qualitative outcomes;
fit and interpret linear and logistic regression, including confounding and interactions;
analyze time-to-event data with Kaplan-Meier, the log-rank test, and the Cox model;
model non-linear and time-dependent effects with flexible survival models;
handle missing data with multiple imputation and Rubin’s rules;
carry out a meta-analysis: effect sizes, fixed- and random-effects models, heterogeneity, and publication bias.





Schedule



No.


Session




1


Introduction to R: environment, projects, scripts, objects and types, import/export, good practices, reproducible reports




2


Data manipulation: filtering, transformation, joins, pivots, dates, strings, recoding, quality control




3


Descriptive statistics and visualization: descriptive statistics, distributions, summary tables, Table 1, graphics, stratification




4


Statistical inference and hypothesis testing: estimation, confidence intervals, tests, effect sizes, power, sample size, quantitative and qualitative comparisons




5


Linear and logistic regression: adjusted coefficients, odds ratios, confounding, interactions, diagnostics, predictions, ROC curve




6


Survival analysis: censoring, Kaplan-Meier, log-rank test, Cox model, hazard ratios, proportional-hazards assumption




7


Flexible survival models: non-linearity, splines, restricted cubic splines, flexible parametric models, time-dependent effects, survival predictions




8


Missing data and multiple imputation: MCAR/MAR/MNAR, complete-case analysis, single and multiple imputation, imputation model, Rubin’s rules, sensitivity analyses




9


Meta-analysis: effect sizes, fixed- and random-effects models, forest plot, heterogeneity, meta-regression, publication bias





Practical information



Audience


Health researchers, clinicians, students; no statistics background required


Prerequisites


None; R/RStudio setup covered in Session 1


Format


Live sessions, slides, notebooks, datasets, exercises

title: METAR
text:
METAR


Conducting Meta-Analysis with REvidence synthesis



 18 hours · 9 sessions · 3 weeks  09/11 – 27/11/2026  200€ (2000 MAD)





Course description
METAR is a practical, methodologically rigorous introduction to conducting meta-analysis with R. It covers the complete evidence-synthesis workflow: formulating a review question, building a search strategy, developing an analysis-ready extraction table, computing effect sizes, fitting fixed-effect and random-effects models, assessing heterogeneity, producing forest plots, exploring moderators, assessing publication bias, rating certainty of evidence, and preparing a reproducible Quarto report.
The course emphasizes transparent reporting, correct interpretation of pooled estimates, reproducibility, and publication-quality tables and figures.


Learning objectives
By the end of METAR, participants will be able to:

formulate a meta-analysis question using the PICO framework and write a review protocol;
build and document a reproducible search and study-selection workflow;
structure extracted study data and risk-of-bias assessments for analysis in R;
compute effect sizes for binary and continuous outcomes;
fit fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analysis models with prediction intervals;
quantify and explore heterogeneity using Q, I², and tau²;
produce publication-quality forest plots and interpret pooled estimates;
conduct subgroup analysis and meta-regression, and assess publication bias;
rate certainty of evidence with GRADE and produce a reproducible Quarto report.





Schedule



No.


Session




1


Systematic reviews and the review protocol: evidence hierarchy, PICO, PRISMA workflow, protocol, eligibility criteria




2


Search strategy and study selection: databases, search strings, deduplication, screening, PRISMA flow diagram




3


Data extraction and risk of bias: extraction tables, risk-of-bias tools, robvis, importing and cleaning data in R, unit harmonization




4


Effect sizes for binary and continuous outcomes: odds ratio, risk ratio, risk difference, mean difference, standardized mean difference, Hedges’ g




5


Fixed-effect and random-effects models: inverse-variance weighting, common-effect model, DerSimonian-Laird, REML, Paule-Mandel, prediction intervals




6


Heterogeneity and sensitivity analysis: Cochran’s Q, I², tau², heterogeneity CIs, Baujat plots, leave-one-out, influence diagnostics




7


Forest plots and result interpretation: forest plot anatomy, study weights, summary diamond, prediction interval, subgroup forest plots




8


Subgroup analysis, meta-regression, and publication bias: bubble plots, funnel plots, Egger/Begg/Peters tests, trim-and-fill




9


Certainty of evidence and reproducible reporting: GRADE, Quarto report, PRISMA diagram, risk-of-bias plot, effect-size table, final project





Practical information



Audience


Clinicians, researchers, PhD students, public health professionals, evidence synthesis analysts


Prerequisites


Basic R recommended, as covered in BIOSTATR
